content: Epidemiological research indicates that a diet rich in marine fatty acids, such as those found in fish oil, may have positive effects on inflammatory conditions like rheumatoid arthritis and potentially asthma. The objective of this review was to evaluate the impact of marine n-3 fatty acid (fish oil) supplementation on asthma and to assess the effects of a diet high in fish oil on asthma outcomes. To gather relevant data, the Cochrane Airways Group Specialised Register was searched, along with bibliographies of retrieved trials. Fish oil manufacturers were also contacted for additional information. The search was up-to-date as of May 2010. The inclusion criteria required randomized controlled trials involving asthma patients aged two years or older, with a study duration of more than four weeks. Double-blind trials were preferred, but single-blind and open trials were also considered. Four reviewers independently assessed the quality of the studies, and inclusion decisions were made by majority vote. The analysis compared marine n-3 fatty acid supplementation with placebo, as there were not enough trials to evaluate dietary changes alone. Nine randomized controlled trials conducted between 1986 and 2001 met the inclusion criteria. Seven of these were parallel-design studies, while two were cross-over studies. Eight trials compared fish oil supplementation with placebo, and one trial compared high-dose versus low-dose marine n-3 fatty acid supplementation. Two studies involved children, while the remaining seven focused on adults. None of the included studies reported outcomes such as asthma exacerbations, health status, or hospital admissions. There was no consistent evidence of improvement in measurable outcomes such as forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), peak flow rate, asthma symptoms, asthma medication use, or bronchial hyperreactivity. However, one study conducted in children, which combined dietary changes with fish oil supplementation, demonstrated improved peak flow and reduced use of asthma medications. Importantly, no adverse events were associated with fish oil supplementation in any of the studies. In conclusion, there is limited evidence to support the recommendation of marine n-3 fatty acid (fish oil) supplementation or dietary modification for improving asthma control. At the same time, there is no evidence to suggest that such supplementation poses any risk to individuals with asthma.
